# How One Brave Dog’s Tumor Trial Is Changing Cancer Treatment for Pets and Children

Image: Beth Wegerer By Beth Wegerer

Published March 3, 2026 5 min read

Alex Mladek/Shutterstock.com

Quick Take The Alternative Treatment That Saved Cla... How Clarice’s Success Can Help Chi... More About the WSU Clinical Trial

## Quick Take

  * Washington State University is currently running clinical trials to test the effectiveness of immunotherapy injections in canine tumors.
  * Clarice was part of the trial and successfully had a tumor removed from her left wrist, avoiding typical leg amputation treatment.
  * Data from the canine trials is helping researchers at Seattle Children’s Hospital apply similar immunotherapy treatments to pediatric brain cancer patients.
  * Current trials, both for canines and humans, are ongoing.

When Jon and Dayla Culp received the news that their six-year-old Labrador retriever, Clarice, had a malignant tumor near her left wrist, the couple was devastated. Dayla had lost her sister, Darcy Klepec, to breast cancer less than two years earlier. Clarice had been a gift from Darcy.

The Culps were told that surgery to remove the tumor would be risky due to its location. It was on a spot near Clarice’s left wrist that didn’t give surgeons much room to work. Plus, the tumor likely extended microscopically beyond what was visible, making it difficult to cleanly remove the cancerous tissue.

Image: Disabled dog three legs standing

Amputation is the usual method of treatment for difficult-to-remove tumors in a dog’s leg.

©golfyinterlude/Shutterstock.com

The recommended treatment was amputation, a common veterinary solution when dogs develop tumors in their extremities that cannot be easily removed. Clarice was already experiencing significant arthritis in her right shoulder. Losing her left leg would mean living with only three legs, a challenge given her existing mobility issues. The Culps wanted a second opinion and turned to Washington State University’s (WSU) Veterinary Teaching Hospital. The family hoped there would be an alternative option available. There was.

## The Alternative Treatment That Saved Clarice

When the Culps met with the vet team at WSU, they learned about a new clinical trial being completed in partnership with Seattle Children’s Hospital. The focus of the trial was to test the efficacy of injecting an immune-stimulating agent directly into tumors in difficult-to-treat locations.

The goal was to stimulate the body’s own immune system by activating T cells. These cells are responsible for physically destroying infected or cancerous cells. The injection would kick-start the body to destroy the hard-to-reach soft tissue sarcoma. The goal was to shrink the tumor enough so that other traditional cancer treatments would be more effective.

The clinical trial was only the first part of Clarice’s treatment plan. The WSU veterinary team combined the trial injection with surgery and radiation for a three-pronged approach. The goal was to eliminate the tumor without removing Clarice’s leg.

Image: veterinarian assistant in protective vest hold down prepare french bulldog to x-ray scanning.

Dogs in the WSU clinical trial often undergo radiation therapy as part of their treatment.

©Try_my_best/Shutterstock.com

One week after receiving the injection, Clarice had surgery to remove most of the tumor. After that, she went through three rounds of radiation therapy to eliminate any residual cancer cells.

Dr. Janean Fidel, a WSU oncologist, oversaw Clarice’s treatment plan. She said that Clarice’s surgery went “as well as anyone expected.” When Clarice returned for her first radiation treatment, there was no tumor that could be felt. Clarice completed her three-round course of radiation therapy by early January 2026. She has since received a clean bill of health and will receive routine checkups to keep an eye on the wrist to ensure the tumor is caught early if it returns.

For the Culp family, having Clarice back home and healthy is their biggest win. They are also grateful that their own dog’s cancer treatment and participation in the clinical trial might be able to help other people and pets. As Jon Culp noted in a recent article about the WSU clinical trial, “In the end, we wanted to do everything we could for Clarice. But knowing her treatment might help someone else someday made the decision feel even more meaningful.”

## How Clarice’s Success Can Help Children with Cancer

The data coming from the WSU trials is being shared with Seattle Children’s Hospital as part of a “comparative oncology” initiative. Canine tumors are biologically very similar to human pediatric brain tumors. The data from WSU’s canine trials is helping researchers design and refine the next phase of human clinical trials at Seattle Children’s Hospital.

WSU and Seattle Children’s Hospital worked together throughout 2024 and 2025 to develop the strategy to combine WSU’s veterinary expertise with the hospital’s pediatric CAR-T cell technology. That technology is being used in active clinical trials underway at the hospital.

Image: Seattle Cityscape Skyline Mount Rainier Aerial View, Washington, USA

Researchers at Seattle Children’s Hospital are using data from the WSU studies in human pediatric cancer treatment trials.

©Engel Ching/Shutterstock.com

Those active trials are part of Seattle Children’s BrainChild series, overseen by Dr. Nicholas Vitanza. CAR-T studies are just one initiative the Vitanza Lab is pursuing for the treatment of children’s cancer. More information about Seattle Children’s immunotherapy work and available clinical trials can be found on the hospital’s Immunotherapy Program page.

## More About the WSU Clinical Trial

The WSU clinical trial, which is ongoing, focuses on local immunotherapy for solid and brain tumors in dogs. Dog owners interested in the program are invited to contact WSU.

Dogs participating in the trial must:

  * Have been diagnosed with an easily accessible soft tissue sarcoma with a minimum tumor size of 2 centimeters.
  * Be a suitable surgery candidate and have undergone all diagnostics considered standard of care.
  * Meet previously set parameters for bloodwork.

The long-term goal of this clinical trial is to add additional immunotherapy treatments to existing canine and human cancer care.

Image: Beth Wegerer

# Welcome to the special hospital where pets are treated better than most human patients

By Rafi Letzter

Image: Animal Medical Center Veterinarian vet veterinary surgery_23

[Input] Sue Maraczi comforts a patient. Rafi Letzter/Business Insider

2016-09-06T21:45:00.000Z

Read in app

Copy link Email Facebook WhatsApp X LinkedIn Bluesky Threads Impact Link

Save Saved

This post includes graphic images of surgery, some of which may be upsetting to readers.

Emergency veterinary medicine is rough work.

"Some people can't take the screaming," said Sue Maraczi, an emergency and critical care nurse at the Animal Medical Center (AMC) on Manhattan's Upper East Side.

Image: Animal Medical Center Veterinarian vet veterinary surgery_27

Rafi Letzter/Business Insider

"But you have to consider that [the animals] are sick, they don't feel well, they're in a weird place, there's unfamiliar faces."

She held a Yorkie in her lap. It didn't need any treatment right that second, but cried pitifully whenever it was left alone in its cage.

Image: Animal Medical Center Veterinarian vet veterinary surgery_11

A team of vets perform surgery to repair a small dog's knee.  Rafi Letzter/Business Insider

Like any big-city hospital, patients show up at AMC's emergency room with problems ranging from sniffles to abuse to horrible injuries. Down the hall in the intensive care unit, a team of veterinarians and technicians care for a small army of critical and terminal creatures.

AMC is the most advanced animal hospital in New York City, and among the most advanced treatment centers anywhere in the country. It's a place where cats and dogs routinely get state-of-the-art radiation treatment for brain cancer, total hip replacements, and even alternative treatments like acupuncture.

One day this summer, I spent 13 hours in the ER: trailing doctors, talking to vets, and watching how they treated the hundreds of animals in the building.

It's an expensive, luxury level of care for people who treat their pets with the same concern that they'd afford a member of their own family, as many AMC veterinarians and staff emphasized.

Image: Animal Medical Center Veterinarian vet veterinary surgery_13

Rafi Letzter/Business Insider

"We get dogs helicoptered in all the time," said Lori Asprea, a technician in internal medicine.

On the day I visited AMC, a cat was released after receiving more than $50,000 in care.

Asprea described one dog that came in with severe leptospirosis, an infection most common in canines but that can jump to humans. When he arrived — on a private jet — his kidneys had already failed. He seemed to recover with treatment, but when it came time to release him back to his owners, a potentially fatal clot clogged up the blood vessels in his lungs, sending him back to the ICU. Another clot killed off flesh on one of his legs.

Today, she said, he runs marathons with his owner.

(Some identifying details, like the names of certain pets, are withheld or altered because of an agreement with AMC intended to protect the identity of the center's patients.)

### ***

Often, pet owners show up at AMC without the cash on hand or insurance to cover emergency treatment.

On the day I visited, a small white dog named Daisy showed up both of her front paws hanging limp. Daisy had leapt off a high curb after her owner and, Maraczi determined, broken both her legs on the asphalt. Treating her would likely cost several thousand dollars, which her owners could not afford to pay.

Image: Animal Medical Center Veterinarian vet veterinary surgery_31

Emergency room veterinarians and technicians tend to Daisy.  Rafi Letzter/Business Insider

Image: Animal Medical Center Veterinarian vet veterinary surgery_41

Rafi Letzter/Business Insider

The next step for AMC staff in this situation is to ask if the owners want to open a line of credit for their pets. Many, especially those who bring in young pets like Daisy with major injuries, say yes.

Image: cat in a CAT scan veterinarian animal medical center

Maia the cat gets a CAT scan. The data will allow St. Vincent to target Maia's nasal tumor.  Rafi Letzter/Tech Insider

And it's clear that they love pushing the boundaries of the possible in veterinary medicine.

Rachel St. Vincent, AMC's radiation oncologist, uses a linear accelerator purchased from a human hospital to finely target and burn away brain tumors and other cancers that resist surgical intervention.

Geoff Hall beats 18-year cancer battle at Mater Hospital
Date: Wed Oct  7 08:00:00 2026 UTC

Geoff Hall, of Biggera Waters, was diagnosed with mantle cell lymphoma in 2008, discovered almost "by accident" during a routine birthday blood test. "I would get a routine blood test once a year," Mr Hall said. "I was travelling to Greece, and when I returned I got the call". Mr Hall lived with the slow-growing blood cancer for years under careful monitoring before eventually requiring treatment. After undergoing multiple rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, doctors said he had exhausted every option. "The doctor told me we're reaching the stage where there was nothing more they could do." "I was headed for palliative care." The RAAF veteran of 22 years, who served postings in Hong Kong, America and across Australia during his career, said the diagnosis was "one of the hardest things" he'd ever faced. His wife of 60 years, Ros, and their cavoodle Chanel, were constant sources of comfort, he said, with his beloved pup sensing when he needed quiet company after treatments. "She'd wait till I sat down, then she'd come and sit beside me and lean against me," he said. "It's amazing what they sense." He said the cancer slowed him down but he was determined to keep fighting and he always trusted his doctors were searching for solutions. Mr Hall's haematologist Dr Rachel Wooldridge secured him a place on a phase 1 clinical trial at the Mater Cancer Care Centre in Brisbane. He began the trial therapy in July last year and his latest bone marrow biopsy and PET scans showed no evidence of cancer and given Mr Hall "a new lease on life". "I was ecstatic," he said. The couple are now planning a trip to the Cook Islands. "I can't wait". Mater Research is extending access to its clinical trials for Gold Coast patients following the healthcare giant's recent acquisition of Gold Coast Private Hospital .

Veterinary oncology
Cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals

Veterinary oncology is a subspecialty of veterinary medicine that deals with cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals. Cancer is a major cause of death in pet animals. In one study, 45% of the dogs that reached 10 years of age or older died of cancer.

Skin tumors are the most frequently diagnosed type of tumor in domestic animals for two reasons: 1. constant exposure of animal skin to the sun and external environment, 2. skin tumors are easy to see because they are on the outside of the animal.

## History

Specialised veterinary oncology training became available in the 21st century.
## Treatment

The most effective method of treating cancer in animals is surgery. Surgery may involve a marginal excision, where just the capsule is excised; wide excision, where a wider area surrounding the capsule (typically 2–3cm) is excised; or radical excision, where the entire compartment is excised, often taking the form of an amputation.
